title: What Would Happen to Our Teeth if Sugar Disappeared?
author: Precision Dental

imageAlt: A woman holding an ice cream and touching her cheek in discomfort
body:
It is a fanciful question with a useful answer, because thinking it through shows exactly which dental problems are caused by sugar and which are not. The results are more mixed than you might expect.

What Would Improve, and Quickly

Tooth Decay Would Fall Sharply

Decay requires bacteria to metabolise fermentable carbohydrate and produce acid. Remove the most readily fermentable source and the acid attacks that dissolve enamel become far less frequent.

We know this is not merely theoretical. Historical populations without access to refined sugar had markedly less decay, and studies of populations whose sugar supply was interrupted during wartime recorded substantial reductions in decay, which reversed once supply resumed.

Children would benefit most, because newly erupted enamel is at its most vulnerable and because childhood is when sugar intake is typically highest. Much of what children's dentistry currently spends its time preventing would simply not arise.

Gum Disease Would Improve Somewhat

Plaque would still form, because bacteria colonise tooth surfaces regardless of diet. Gingivitis and periodontitis are driven by the body's inflammatory response to that plaque rather than by sugar directly, so gum disease would not disappear.

It would likely improve at the margins, though, since high-sugar diets support plaque accumulation and contribute to systemic inflammation. Daily cleaning and gum and periodontal treatment would still be necessary.

What Would Not Change

Erosion

Acidic foods and drinks dissolve enamel directly, with no bacterial involvement. Citrus, vinegar, wine, kombucha and sugar-free soft drinks would all continue doing exactly what they do now. Reflux would continue to erode teeth from the inside.

Erosion is already an increasing problem, and in a sugar-free world it would become the dominant form of tooth surface loss.

Wear From Grinding

Grinding and clenching has nothing to do with diet. Stress, sleep disorders and bite factors would continue to flatten, chip and crack teeth.

Cracks, Trauma and Injury

Broken teeth from sport, falls and biting something hard would be unaffected.

Starches Would Partly Fill the Gap

This is the catch. Cooked starches break down into fermentable sugars in the mouth, so bread, crackers, crisps and pasta still feed the same bacteria, particularly when they linger in the grooves of molars. Decay rates would fall substantially, but they would not reach zero.

Wisdom Teeth, Alignment and Development

None of these have any dietary cause in the sense sugar does.

What It Tells Us

The useful conclusion is that sugar is the main driver of one disease, not of dentistry as a whole. Even in a world without it, teeth would still need cleaning, gums would still need care, and people would still crack molars on olive stones.

It also highlights the difference between frequency and quantity. Since sugar is not going anywhere, the practical version of this thought experiment is to reduce the number of separate occasions it reaches your teeth. Each exposure starts an acid cycle of 20 to 40 minutes, so six nibbles do far more harm than one serving.

The Opposite Thought Experiment

It is also worth running the question the other way: what if nothing changed except that everyone cleaned between their teeth every day?

Decay between teeth, which is one of the most common sites and one that neither you nor a toothbrush can reach, would fall considerably. Gingivitis would improve in most people within a fortnight. The progression from gingivitis to periodontitis, which accounts for most adult tooth loss, would slow for a great many people.

That version of the experiment is not fanciful at all. It costs a few dollars and three minutes a day, and it is available to everybody right now.

Why the Question Is Worth Asking

Thought experiments like this one are useful because they isolate variables. Dental advice often arrives as an undifferentiated list, with sugar, brushing, flossing, acid, grinding and regular visits all presented as equally important for everything.

They are not. Sugar frequency drives decay. Plaque left undisturbed drives gum disease. Acid drives erosion. Force drives wear and fracture. Each has its own cause and its own countermeasure, and knowing which problem you are actually prone to tells you where to put your effort.

That is part of what a thorough examination is for: working out which of these applies to you, rather than giving everybody the same advice.

The Practical Translation

  • Keep sweet foods and drinks to mealtimes rather than grazing
  • Make water the default drink between meals
  • Remember that sugar-free does not mean acid-free
  • Clean between your teeth daily, since plaque would form in any dietary scenario
  • Have early decay found at a check-up and clean, when it may need only a small white filling or may still be reversible

faq.q: Would tooth decay disappear without sugar?
a: It would fall sharply, but not vanish, because cooked starches also break down into fermentable sugars in the mouth.
Not directly. Gum disease is driven by the body's response to plaque, although high-sugar diets support plaque build-up.

faq.q: What damages teeth apart from sugar?
a: Acid erosion from food and drinks, grinding and clenching, and cracks or injuries from trauma.

faq.q: Are starchy foods bad for teeth?
a: Bread, crackers and crisps break down into sugars in the mouth, particularly when they stick to the teeth, so frequency still matters.

faq.q: Is reducing how often I eat sugar better than cutting the amount?
a: For teeth, reducing the number of occasions usually helps more, because each exposure starts a new acid attack.

faq.q: What is the single most useful daily habit for teeth?
a: Cleaning between your teeth every day, alongside twice-daily brushing with fluoride toothpaste.
